chunk_findings.detail: The span extractor `_spans()` does collect the new README text `` `ddflow --agent <holder> heartbeat <id>` `` (README.md, the lapsed-lease remedy), but the check's regex `r"ddflow ([a-z][a-z-]*)(?: ([a-z][a-z-]*))?"` only matches when a lowercase command word follows `ddflow ` *directly*. For that span, `re.match` returns `None` (the next character is `-`), so the loop takes the `if not m: continue` branch and the span is never validated at all. Concretely: if the real subcommand were `heartbeat <id>` on some other command, or if `heartbeat` were renamed/removed, this test — whose entire job is "every command the README names exists" — still passes, because every flag-first invocation form (`ddflow --agent … <cmd> …`, `ddflow -v <cmd>`, `ddflow <path> <cmd>`) is silently exempted rather than parsed. The same blind spot means the companion completeness test (`test_every_cli_command_is_named_in_the_readme` at line 36) and this one give contradictory verdicts for such a line: line 36 searches for the literal `ddflow heartbeat` (which does not occur in `ddflow --agent <holder> heartbeat <id>`), while line 52 skips the line entirely, so a command documented only in the flag-first form the change itself introduces is simultaneously "missing" from one test's perspective and unvalidated by the other.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_readme_catchup.py:52 (`test_every_command_the_readme_names_exists`)

chunk_findings.detail: The paragraph asserts the registry accepts the artefact when `<!-- mcp-name: io.github/delian/ddflow-mcp -->` is present and the OCI label `io.modelcontextprotocol.server.name` carries "the same name". The MCP registry server name is a reverse-DNS namespace, then `/`, then the server name in the final segment (e.g. `io.github.delian/ddflow-mcp`) — the namespace must be dot-separated, `io.github` alone is the reserved GitHub-namespace prefix, and the segment after the slash may not itself contain a slash. `io.github/delian/ddflow-mcp` therefore parses as namespace `io.github` with name `delian/ddflow-mcp`, which the registry rejects on publish. Any user following this paragraph (and any `test_registry_ownership.py` that only checks the README marker against `server.json`, i.e. two copies of the same malformed string) will get a release that passes CI locally and is refused by the registry — the exact failure the paragraph claims is prevented. The correct string is `io.github.delian/ddflow-mcp`, in both the README marker and the image label.
chunk_findings.title: README.md:811 (registry-ownership paragraph)

chunk_findings.detail: The new test is supposed to guarantee that the README "names only real commands", but `_spans()` only returns strings that literally begin with `ddflow `, so any command the README names without the CLI prefix is never validated. The paragraph added by this same change names four commands in exactly that unprefixed form — `` `recover --item` ``, `` `release --note salvaged` ``, `` `claim` ``, and `doctor` — to say nothing of the two argument forms (`--item`, `--note salvaged`) and the `--force` flag used a few lines later. Concretely, if the real command were `reclaim` (or the flag were `--id`), the README would instruct the reader to run a command that does not exist, and both `test_every_command_the_readme_names_exists` (the span never enters `_spans()`) and `test_every_cli_command_is_named_in_the_readme` (which only checks that *real* commands appear as `ddflow <name>`) would still pass; only the MCP-tool regex is prefix-independent. The change therefore ships the very class of defect — a named command/flag that is not checked against the parser — that its stated purpose is to prevent, specifically in the sentence it adds.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_readme_catchup.py:30 (test_every_command_the_readme_names_exists / `_spans`)

chunk_findings.detail: The row now pairs CLI `... research ...` with MCP tool `ddflow_research_add`, while the sibling record commands are paired verb-for-verb (`lesson add` → `ddflow_lesson_add`, `decision add` → `ddflow_decision_add`) and variants are wildcarded (`bug found|fixed` → `ddflow_bug_*`). Because the CLI column for research exposes no `add` subcommand, the tool naming convention used throughout this table maps `research` to `ddflow_research`, not `ddflow_research_add`. If the shipped tool is `ddflow_research`, this line names a tool that does not exist (exactly the class of error the new `tests/test_readme_catchup.py` is meant to catch); if the shipped tool really is `ddflow_research_add`, then the CLI cell is wrong for omitting `add`. Either way the row is internally inconsistent, and the change introduces that inconsistency by editing only the tool cell.
chunk_findings.title: README.md:172 (record bullet, MCP tool column)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_spans()` only ever returns text that literally starts with `ddflow ` (the inline regex requires the `ddflow ` prefix at line 30, and the fenced-block branch requires `ln.startswith("ddflow ")` at line 35), and `test_every_command_the_readme_names_exists` then inspects only the first one or two lower-case words of that span (line 57), never flags. So every remedy the *same diff* adds in the form the hook actually prints is invisible to the test:

* `recover --item`, `release --note salvaged`, `claim` — they have no `ddflow ` prefix, so `_spans()` drops them and they are never compared to the parser at all (contrast `ddflow --agent <holder> heartbeat <id>` in the same sentence, which *is* checked because of the prefix).
* `--force` (line "…and `--force` replaces the generated hook") and `--claude` in `ddflow hooks install --claude` are flags; the test only checks `hooks` and `install`, so a flag that does not exist on `hooks install` passes.
* The same applies to `doctor` / `hooks install` as written unprefixed in this paragraph.

Concretely: if the real `recover`/`release` accept `--id`/`--reason` rather than `--item`/`--note`, `_spans()` yields no span containing them, `test_every_command_the_readme_names_exists` stays green, and the README keeps naming a flag that does not exist — exactly the class of error the PR intent says this test is meant to catch ("any named command/flag/tool that does not exist"). The test's own docstring ("names real commands") and the stated purpose are therefore not met by the code at lines 27–37/57.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_spans()` deliberately returns the *entire* `ddflow …` span for a line, and `test_every_command_the_readme_names_exists` parses only the **first** invocation out of that span (`re.match(r"ddflow ([a-z][a-z-]*)(?: ([a-z][a-z-]*))?", span)`), picks `parser = subs[sub] … else top[cmd]` from it, and then validates *every* `--flag` it can find in the whole span against that one parser's `known` set. A span that contains a chained second command therefore has its flags checked against the wrong command, and a valid README line gets reported as invalid.

Concrete input: a fenced/inline line such as

    `ddflow config get --key && ddflow mcp serve --port 1`

(`_spans` returns the whole string; there is no `\s{2,}` gap, so `re.split(r"\s{2,}", span)[0]` keeps all of it). The match yields `cmd="config"`, `sub="get"`, so `known` is the option set of `ddflow config get`; the flag scan then also finds `--port`, which belongs to `ddflow mcp serve`, and appends `… [--port is not an option of \`ddflow config\`]`, failing the test on a correct README. Symmetrically, the second invocation is never checked for existence at all (its `cmd`/`sub` are ignored), so a bogus command in the second half of a chained example slips through. Any single-line example using `&&`, `;`, or `|` to join two `ddflow` invocations triggers this.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_readme_catchup.py:76 (flag validation loop in `test_every_command_the_readme_names_exists`)

chunk_findings.detail: The "names every top-level command" check uses `re.search(rf"ddflow {re.escape(c)}\b", flat)`. `\b` is satisfied by a hyphen, because a hyphen is a non-word character. So a command name that is a prefix of another command's name is considered "named" whenever the longer name appears. Concretely, if the CLI has both `config` and `config-get` as top-level commands and the README only ever writes ``ddflow config-get``, then `flat` contains `ddflow config-get`, and `re.search(r"ddflow config\b", "ddflow config-get")` matches (the boundary is between `g` and `-`). The list comprehension therefore yields an empty `missing` and the test passes even though the top-level command `config` is never documented — exactly the regression this test exists to catch. The same missing trailing boundary exists in the flag pattern `(?<![\w-])(--[a-z][a-z-]*)`, so a documented `--foo_bar` is read as `--foo` and silently accepted when `--foo` happens to exist. The predicate needs a negative lookahead, e.g. `ddflow {c}(?![\w-])` (and `(?![\w-])` after the flag match), rather than `\b`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_readme_catchup.py:47 (`test_every_cli_command_is_named_in_the_readme`)
